question: For two evenly-matched teams on a neutral floor, what are the odds of leading (and winning) at the end of each quarter?
headline: Two even teams are a coin flip at tip; a lead is worth much more late than early - up 6 after Q1 wins ~66%, the same 6 after Q3 wins ~75%.
read: Even teams are rarely separated early - 61% of games are still within a possession or two of level after Q1 - and they steadily pull apart. By the final buzzer only 36% of even games finish within 6, and 45% finish 11 or more apart. Double-digit finals are the norm even between equals, because scoring noise compounds.
A lead is worth more the later you hold it: up 6 is worth about 66% after Q1, 74% by half and 75% after Q3 - the same six points, very different security depending on how much clock is left.

Useful caveat for late leads: a smooth random-walk model says an end-Q3 lead of 6 should be worth about 86%; the games themselves say 75%. Comebacks happen more than the model predicts - fouling, 3-point variance and coasting give the trailing team fatter tails. Quote the measured number, not the model, for late-game leads.
caveats: Even-team identification is via a between/within margin-variance decomposition, not a clean spread filter: the play-by-play pregame-spread column is a constant junk value and cannot identify an even matchup.

The conditional win probability is pooled over all games, a mix of even and mismatched. Conditioning on the current lead absorbs most of the strength information, but a leader is on average the better team, so these read slightly high for a genuinely even pair.
Neutral court: home advantage is symmetrized out. In the real data home teams win 55.5% with an average margin of +2.1. If one even team is at home, treat it as roughly that much in its favour.
No player, injury or rest context - this is the league-average even matchup, the ground-floor baseline to reason from.
